module.title: Predicate Logic
module.description: Module 2 introduces predicate logic (first-order logic): predicates and propositional functions, the universal and existential quantifiers, the domain of discourse, the standard translation patterns between English and quantified logic, De Morgan's laws for quantifiers, and the rules for nested quantifiers — including why the order of ∀ and ∃ matters and how to negate any nested-quantifier expression.

lessons.title: Predicates and Quantifiers
lessons.welcome: Welcome to Module 2. Propositional logic from Module 1 was powerful, but it could not say things like 'every integer has a successor' or 'some student passed the exam'. To talk about objects in a domain and the properties they share, we need PREDICATE LOGIC — sometimes called first-order logic. In this lesson you will meet predicates, the universe of discourse, and the two quantifiers ∀ ('for all') and ∃ ('there exists') that turn open sentences into propositions.
objectives: Define a predicate (propositional function) and explain how it differs from a proposition.
Identify the domain (universe of discourse) of a predicate and evaluate the predicate on specific values.
Use the universal quantifier ∀ to express 'for every' statements.
Use the existential quantifier ∃ to express 'there exists' statements.
Determine the truth value of a quantified statement on small finite domains.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: In Module 1 I learned that 'x + 1 = 2' is not a proposition because x is free. So how do mathematicians ever write equations like that?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: They use predicates. We call 'x + 1 = 2' a propositional function P(x). It is not yet a proposition, but the moment we plug in a value, or attach a quantifier, it becomes one.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: So P(1) is the proposition '1 + 1 = 2', which is true?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Exactly. And P(5) is the proposition '5 + 1 = 2', which is false. Predicates are templates; you fill them in to get propositions.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: What if I want to talk about all values of x at once?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Then you use a quantifier. ∀x P(x) says 'P holds for every x'. ∃x P(x) says 'P holds for at least one x'. These two symbols are the heart of predicate logic.

sections.heading: Why Propositional Logic Is Not Enough
sections.explanation:
Propositional logic treats sentences as black boxes named p, q, r. It cannot look inside a sentence and reason about its objects. Consider the classic argument:

  All men are mortal.
  Socrates is a man.
  Therefore, Socrates is mortal.

In propositional logic, those three sentences are just p, q, r — three unrelated atoms. There is no way to express the shared structure that lets us draw the conclusion. We need a language that talks about OBJECTS (Socrates, men), PROPERTIES of those objects (being mortal, being a man), and QUANTITIES ('all', 'some'). That language is predicate logic.
examples: Propositional logic cannot express 'every integer has an additive inverse' as a single statement.
Propositional logic cannot link 'Socrates is a man' to 'all men are mortal' to derive 'Socrates is mortal'.
common_mistakes: Trying to model 'every x' by introducing one propositional variable per element of the domain. That works only for finite domains and quickly explodes; quantifiers handle infinite or large domains in one stroke.

visual_idea.description: A side-by-side picture: on the left, three opaque propositional letters p, q, r with no internal structure; on the right, predicate logic with three labelled boxes showing 'object', 'predicate', and 'quantifier' that link to one another. The contrast emphasizes that predicate logic looks INSIDE a sentence.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click any sentence on the right and the diagram highlights its objects (in green) and its predicate (in orange).

sections.heading: Predicates and Propositional Functions
sections.explanation:
A PREDICATE (also called a propositional function) is a sentence that contains one or more free variables. We write predicates with capital letters and list the variables in parentheses. Examples:

  • P(x): 'x > 0'
  • M(x): 'x is mortal'
  • R(x, y, z): 'x + y = z'

On its own, a predicate has no truth value. It becomes a PROPOSITION as soon as every free variable is replaced by a specific element from the domain.

  P(3) = '3 > 0'   →  TRUE
  P(-1) = '-1 > 0' →  FALSE
  R(2, 3, 5)        →  TRUE
  R(2, 3, 6)        →  FALSE

The number of arguments a predicate takes is its ARITY. P(x) is unary; R(x, y, z) is ternary. Predicates can also take zero arguments — those are just ordinary propositions.
examples: Let Q(x, y) mean 'x = y + 3'. Then Q(5, 2) is the proposition '5 = 2 + 3', which is true.
Let Even(x) mean 'x is even'. Even(8) is true; Even(7) is false; Even(x) by itself has no truth value.
common_mistakes: Treating a predicate as a proposition. A predicate is a TEMPLATE; it has no truth value until variables are bound or assigned.
Confusing a predicate's name with its arity. P(x) and P(x, y) are different predicates even if they share the letter P.

visual_idea.description: A 'fill-in card' visual: a predicate P(x) is drawn as a blank fill-in slot. The learner drags a value onto the slot, and the card flips to show the resulting proposition along with its truth value (T/F).
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Provide a small bank of values to drag in. Right answers snap into the slot; wrong-typed values (e.g., a string for an integer predicate) bounce back.

sections.heading: The Domain of Discourse
sections.explanation:
Every predicate must be evaluated against a DOMAIN (also called the universe of discourse), often denoted U. The domain is the set of objects the variables can take values from. The same predicate can have different truth values on different domains.

Example: let P(x) be 'x² ≥ 0'.
  • If U = ℝ (the real numbers), P(x) is true for every x.
  • If U includes complex numbers like i, P(i) = 'i² ≥ 0' is false (since i² = −1).

Always state the domain. A quantified statement without a domain is incomplete and may have no clear truth value.
examples: Domain = positive integers, P(n) = 'n is prime'. Then P(2), P(3), P(5) are true; P(4), P(6) are false.
Domain = students in your class, S(x) = 'x has a laptop'. Each S(student) is a concrete proposition once you name the student.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to specify the domain. The truth value of ∀x P(x) depends critically on what x ranges over.
Using a domain that is too broad and accidentally including objects the predicate is not meant for (e.g., including non-numbers when P(x) compares numbers).

visual_idea.description: A horizontal strip labelled U with a row of object icons (numbers, students, books, etc.). Above each object the predicate's truth value is shown in green or red. Switching the dropdown for the domain re-populates the strip.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Toggle between several preset domains (positive integers, real numbers, students-in-class) and watch the truth values reshuffle for the same predicate.

sections.heading: The Universal Quantifier ∀
sections.explanation:
The universal quantifier is written ∀ (an upside-down A). The statement

  ∀x P(x)

reads 'for every x, P(x)' or 'for all x, P(x)'. It is TRUE exactly when P(x) holds for EVERY value of x in the domain. It is FALSE if there is even one x in the domain — called a COUNTEREXAMPLE — for which P(x) is false.

On a finite domain U = {a₁, a₂, …, aₙ}, the universal quantifier is just a long conjunction:

  ∀x P(x) ≡ P(a₁) ∧ P(a₂) ∧ … ∧ P(aₙ).

On the empty domain, ∀x P(x) is VACUOUSLY TRUE — there are no elements to fail the predicate.
examples: Domain = ℝ. ∀x (x² ≥ 0) is TRUE — every real squared is non-negative.
Domain = ℤ. ∀n (n² > 0) is FALSE — counterexample n = 0.
Domain = students in your class. ∀x (x has a laptop) is true only if every single student does.
common_mistakes: Believing one example proves a universal claim. ∀x P(x) requires P to hold for every x; one example is never enough.
Believing one counterexample is not enough to disprove. A single x where P(x) fails is sufficient to disprove ∀x P(x).

visual_idea.description: A row showing the domain elements as columns. Each column displays the truth value of P(x) for that element. The ∀ verdict at the right turns green only if every column is green.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Flip any single cell to red and watch the ∀ verdict instantly turn red — a tactile reminder that one counterexample is enough.

sections.heading: The Existential Quantifier ∃
sections.explanation:
The existential quantifier is written ∃ (a backwards E). The statement

  ∃x P(x)

reads 'there exists an x such that P(x)' or 'for some x, P(x)'. It is TRUE if at least one element of the domain satisfies P, and FALSE only if NO element satisfies P.

On a finite domain U = {a₁, a₂, …, aₙ}, the existential quantifier is a long disjunction:

  ∃x P(x) ≡ P(a₁) ∨ P(a₂) ∨ … ∨ P(aₙ).

On the empty domain, ∃x P(x) is FALSE — there is nothing to witness P.

A close cousin you will sometimes see is the UNIQUENESS QUANTIFIER ∃! ('there is exactly one x'). It says both existence AND uniqueness: at least one x works, and no two different x's both work.
examples: Domain = ℤ. ∃n (n² = 4) is TRUE — n = 2 or n = -2 work.
Domain = ℤ. ∃n (n² = 2) is FALSE — no integer squared equals 2.
Domain = ℝ. ∃!x (x + 5 = 8) is TRUE with the unique witness x = 3.
common_mistakes: Reading 'there exists' as 'every'. ∃ asks for at least one witness, not all.
Failing to give a witness when one is required to prove ∃x P(x). Concrete examples settle existential claims.

visual_idea.description: Same domain row as the ∀ visual, but the ∃ verdict turns green as soon as at least one column is green; flips back to red only when every column is red.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Add a 'witness highlighter' that ringed the first true column to remind the learner that ONE witness suffices for ∃.

worked_examples.problem: Domain = integers. State the truth value of each: (a) ∀n (n² ≥ 0). (b) ∃n (n² = 2). (c) ∀n (2n > n). (d) ∃n (n² < 0).
step_by_step_solution: (a) Pick any integer n. n² is the product of two equal-signed numbers, so it is ≥ 0. True for every integer ⇒ ∀ holds.
(b) We need an integer whose square is 2. The candidates ±1 give 1, and ±2 give 4. No integer squared equals 2. False.
(c) Look for a counterexample. n = 0 gives 0 > 0, which is false. So ∀ fails.
(d) Squares of integers are always ≥ 0. There is no integer with a negative square. False.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each ∀ requires verification on every element; each ∃ requires only one witness. Counterexamples decisively settle ∀; missing witnesses settle ∃ in the negative.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Answering (c) TRUE because the inequality holds for positive n. Always check n = 0 and negative integers when the domain is all integers.

worked_examples.problem: Let R(x, y, z) denote 'x + y = z' over the integers. Determine the truth value of R(2, -1, 1), R(3, 4, 7), and R(x, 3, z).
step_by_step_solution: R(2, -1, 1) becomes 2 + (-1) = 1, which is true.
R(3, 4, 7) becomes 3 + 4 = 7, which is true.
R(x, 3, z) still has two free variables; it is not a proposition until x and z are bound or assigned.
worked_examples.final_answer: R(2, -1, 1) = TRUE. R(3, 4, 7) = TRUE. R(x, 3, z) is NOT a proposition (open sentence with free x, z).
worked_examples.why_it_works: A predicate produces a proposition only when ALL of its free variables receive values.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calling R(x, 3, z) true or false. With free variables it has no truth value — it is still a predicate.

quick_checks.question: P(x) is 'x is even', domain is the positive integers. P(7) is:
quick_checks.explanation: 7 is odd, so P(7) is the false proposition '7 is even'.

quick_checks.question: On the empty domain, ∀x P(x) is true and ∃x P(x) is false.
quick_checks.explanation: The universal is vacuously true (no failing elements) and the existential is false (no witness).

quick_checks.question: Domain = real numbers. Which of these is FALSE?
quick_checks.explanation: Counterexample x = 0 gives 0 > 0, which is false.

key_takeaways: A predicate P(x) is a sentence with free variables; it is not a proposition until variables are bound.
The domain (universe of discourse) is the set the variables range over; always state it.
∀x P(x) is true exactly when P holds for every element of the domain; one counterexample disproves it.
∃x P(x) is true exactly when at least one element of the domain satisfies P; no witness disproves it.
On a finite domain, ∀ behaves like a long ∧ and ∃ behaves like a long ∨.
summary.next: Next we learn the standard patterns for translating English sentences into quantified logic, and how to negate any quantified statement using De Morgan's laws for quantifiers.

lessons.title: Translating and Negating Quantified Statements
lessons.welcome: Knowing the symbols ∀ and ∃ is only half the skill. The other half is FLUENT TRANSLATION between English and predicate logic. In this lesson you will master two essential patterns ('all A are B' and 'some A is B'), learn how the choice of domain shapes a translation, and pick up De Morgan's laws for quantifiers — the rule that lets you negate any quantified statement in one stroke.
objectives: Translate 'All A are B' as ∀x (A(x) → B(x)) and 'Some A is B' as ∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x)).
Choose a domain that simplifies a translation and switch between domain choices when needed.
Apply De Morgan's laws for quantifiers: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).
Push negations inward through quantifier chains until they touch only predicates.
Express the negation of a quantified English sentence back in clear English.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why is 'All cats purr' written ∀x (C(x) → P(x)) and not ∀x (C(x) ∧ P(x))?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Because ∀x (C(x) ∧ P(x)) would say every object in the domain is both a cat AND purrs — including the chairs and the math professors. The implication form filters: 'IF x is a cat, THEN x purrs', which is exactly what the English means.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: And why does 'Some cat purrs' use ∧ instead of →?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Because ∃x (C(x) → P(x)) is true the moment we find anything that is not a cat — the implication is vacuously satisfied. We want a real witness: an x that is a cat AND purrs. Conjunction is the right choice.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: How do I negate something like 'every student passed'?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Push the negation past the quantifier. ¬(every passed) becomes 'some did not pass'. That is exactly De Morgan's law for quantifiers.

sections.heading: The Two Standard Translation Patterns
sections.explanation:
Almost every quantified English sentence fits one of two patterns. Memorize them:

  PATTERN A — 'All As are Bs' ⇒ ∀x (A(x) → B(x)).
  PATTERN B — 'Some A is a B' ⇒ ∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x)).

The asymmetry is intentional. With ∀ we use → because we want to constrain only the As; non-As make the implication vacuously true. With ∃ we use ∧ because we want a witness that simultaneously belongs to A and to B.
examples: 'All birds fly' → ∀x (Bird(x) → Fly(x)).
'Some student is tired' → ∃x (Student(x) ∧ Tired(x)).
'No mammal lays eggs' (a 'No A is B' negates an existential): ¬∃x (Mammal(x) ∧ Lays(x)) ≡ ∀x (Mammal(x) → ¬Lays(x)).
common_mistakes: Using ∧ inside ∀: ∀x (A(x) ∧ B(x)) wrongly forces every domain element to be an A — usually false.
Using → inside ∃: ∃x (A(x) → B(x)) is satisfied by any non-A and rarely captures the intended meaning.

visual_idea.description: Two side-by-side cards, one for ∀ and one for ∃. Each card shows the WRONG translation in red, the RIGHT translation in green, and a one-line reason underneath.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Hover over the wrong form and the page shows a tiny counterexample (e.g., 'with ∀ ∧, this becomes false because the chair is not a cat').

sections.heading: Choosing a Domain
sections.explanation:
The same English sentence can be translated different ways depending on the domain. Two equivalent options are common:

  (i) RESTRICTED DOMAIN — the domain itself includes only objects you care about (e.g., U = students). The translation is shorter because the 'is a student' part disappears.

  (ii) UNRESTRICTED DOMAIN — the domain is large (e.g., U = all people). You need an extra predicate ('is a student') to filter.

Both are correct, but the choice affects readability.
examples: 'Some student in your class is friendly.'  Domain = students in your class: ∃x F(x).  Domain = all people: ∃x (S(x) ∧ F(x)).
'Every student in your class can speak Hindi.'  Domain = students: ∀x H(x).  Domain = all people: ∀x (S(x) → H(x)).
common_mistakes: Mixing the two styles inside one formula. Pick a domain at the start and stay with it.
Forgetting the filtering predicate when the domain is unrestricted, ending up with a wrong translation.

visual_idea.description: Two parallel renderings of the same English sentence: 'restricted-domain' translation on top, 'unrestricted-domain' translation below, with arrows showing how the filter predicate appears or disappears.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Toggle the domain and watch the formula re-render in real time.

sections.heading: De Morgan's Laws for Quantifiers
sections.explanation:
Negation flips a quantifier. Two rules cover everything:

  ¬∀x P(x)  ≡  ∃x ¬P(x)
  ¬∃x P(x)  ≡  ∀x ¬P(x)

In English: 'not every x is P' is the same as 'some x is not P'; and 'no x is P' is the same as 'every x is not P'. These are the natural extensions of the propositional De Morgan's laws to infinite-style conjunctions and disjunctions.
examples: ¬∀x (x is healthy) ≡ ∃x ¬(x is healthy) — 'someone is unhealthy.'
¬∃x (x can keep a secret) ≡ ∀x ¬(x can keep a secret) — 'no one can keep a secret.'
¬∀n (n is prime) ≡ ∃n ¬(n is prime) — 'some n is not prime.'
common_mistakes: Negating a ∀ to a ∀ ('every x is not P') without flipping the quantifier. Always flip ∀ to ∃ and vice versa.
Forgetting to negate the inner predicate when flipping the quantifier.

visual_idea.description: A two-step flowchart starting from ¬∀x P(x). Step 1: flip the quantifier to ∃. Step 2: move ¬ inside, negating P(x). Final result: ∃x ¬P(x).
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Animate the negation symbol sliding inward through the quantifier so the flip is felt visually.

sections.heading: Pushing Negations Inward
sections.explanation:
When you have a complex quantified expression, the standard discipline is to push the negation as far INWARD as possible — until ¬ touches only atomic predicates. Use De Morgan's laws repeatedly:

  ¬∀x P(x)        ⇒ ∃x ¬P(x)
  ¬∃x P(x)        ⇒ ∀x ¬P(x)
  ¬(P(x) ∧ Q(x))  ⇒ ¬P(x) ∨ ¬Q(x)
  ¬(P(x) ∨ Q(x))  ⇒ ¬P(x) ∧ ¬Q(x)
  ¬(P → Q)        ⇒ P ∧ ¬Q

After all moves, the formula expresses the SAME meaning as the negation but is much easier to translate back into natural English.
examples: ¬∀x (D(x) → O(x)) — 'not every driver obeys' — push: ∃x ¬(D(x) → O(x)) ≡ ∃x (D(x) ∧ ¬O(x)) — 'some driver does not obey'.
¬∃x (S(x) ∧ ¬L(x)) — 'no student lacks a laptop' — push: ∀x ¬(S(x) ∧ ¬L(x)) ≡ ∀x (¬S(x) ∨ L(x)) ≡ ∀x (S(x) → L(x)).
common_mistakes: Stopping halfway (e.g., leaving ¬∃ unsimplified). Always push ¬ until it touches only predicates.
Forgetting that ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q, NOT P → ¬Q.

visual_idea.description: A vertical chain showing each step of pushing ¬ inward. Each rewrite is labelled with the rule applied (De Morgan for quantifiers, De Morgan for ∧/∨, implication-as-disjunction).
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Step button: each click applies one rewrite and highlights the rule used. Lets the learner build the derivation manually.

worked_examples.problem: Translate 'No student in your class has taken a course in logic programming' two ways: (i) with domain = students in your class, (ii) with domain = all people. Use L(x) = 'x has taken logic programming' and S(x) = 'x is a student in your class'.
step_by_step_solution: (i) Restricted domain. 'No student has taken' = ¬∃x L(x), or equivalently ∀x ¬L(x).
(ii) Unrestricted domain. We must filter to students: ¬∃x (S(x) ∧ L(x)).
Push the negation: ∀x ¬(S(x) ∧ L(x)) ≡ ∀x (¬S(x) ∨ ¬L(x)) ≡ ∀x (S(x) → ¬L(x)).
worked_examples.why_it_works: On the restricted domain there is nothing to filter. On the unrestricted domain we use S(x) inside an implication to focus the claim on students only.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing ∀x (S(x) ∧ ¬L(x)) for the unrestricted domain. That asserts every person in the world is a student — and did not take logic programming. Wrong meaning.

worked_examples.problem: Express the negation of 'Some drivers do not obey the speed limit' so that ¬ touches only predicates. Use D(x) = 'x is a driver' and O(x) = 'x obeys the speed limit'.
step_by_step_solution: Original: ∃x (D(x) ∧ ¬O(x)).
Negate: ¬∃x (D(x) ∧ ¬O(x)).
Flip ∃ to ∀ and push: ∀x ¬(D(x) ∧ ¬O(x)).
De Morgan inside: ∀x (¬D(x) ∨ O(x)).
Rewrite as implication: ∀x (D(x) → O(x)).
worked_examples.why_it_works: Pushing ¬ all the way inward leaves a clean form whose English reading is 'every driver obeys the speed limit'.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing ∀x (D(x) ∧ O(x)) — that wrongly claims every object in the domain is a driver.

worked_examples.problem: Use quantifiers to express: 'Lois has asked Professor Michaels a question.' Predicates: A(x, y) = 'x has asked y a question'.
step_by_step_solution: Lois and Professor Michaels are specific individuals — constants.
Plug into the predicate: A(Lois, Michaels).
worked_examples.why_it_works: Quantifiers are needed only when a variable ranges over the domain. With named individuals, we apply the predicate directly.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Inventing a quantifier where none is needed: ∃x A(x, Michaels) loses the information that the asker is specifically Lois.

quick_checks.question: 'Every cat purrs' translates to:
quick_checks.explanation: 'All A are B' uses → inside ∀; the conjunction form would force every domain element to be a cat.

quick_checks.question: Negate ∀x ∃y P(x, y) so that ¬ touches only predicates:
quick_checks.explanation: Flip each quantifier and push ¬ inward step by step.

quick_checks.question: 'No A is B' is equivalent to ∀x (A(x) → ¬B(x)).

key_takeaways: 'All A are B' translates to ∀x (A(x) → B(x)); 'Some A is B' translates to ∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x)).
Choosing a restricted domain removes the filter predicate; an unrestricted domain requires it.
De Morgan's laws for quantifiers: ¬∀ ↔ ∃¬ and ¬∃ ↔ ∀¬.
Always push negations inward until ¬ only touches atomic predicates.
summary.next: Next we tackle the trickiest part of predicate logic: NESTED quantifiers, where the order of ∀ and ∃ can completely change the meaning of a sentence.

lessons.title: Nested Quantifiers and Order
lessons.welcome: Most interesting mathematical statements use TWO OR MORE quantifiers stacked together. The definition of a limit, additive inverse, surjectivity, every database join condition — they all involve nested quantifiers. The single most important rule to remember: ORDER MATTERS. Swapping ∀ and ∃ can turn a true statement into a false one. In this lesson you will read nested quantifiers as nested loops, learn the four standard patterns, translate complex math sentences, and negate any nested expression.
objectives: Read ∀x ∀y, ∀x ∃y, ∃x ∀y, and ∃x ∃y as nested loops over the domain.
Distinguish ∀x ∃y P(x, y) from ∃y ∀x P(x, y) and explain why the second is strictly stronger.
Translate complex mathematical statements such as 'every real has an additive inverse' into nested-quantifier form.
Negate any nested-quantifier expression by flipping each quantifier and negating the inner predicate.
Recognize implicit quantifiers in everyday math language and make them explicit.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Are ∀x ∃y P(x, y) and ∃y ∀x P(x, y) really different?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Almost always. Let P(x, y) mean 'x + y = 0' over the reals. ∀x ∃y P(x, y) says: for every x, there is SOME y that zeros it out — true, take y = −x. ∃y ∀x P(x, y) says: there is ONE y that zeros out every x — false, no single number is the inverse of every real.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: So in ∀x ∃y, the y can depend on x?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Exactly. The inner y is chosen AFTER x is fixed, so it can be a function of x. In ∃y ∀x, the y is fixed FIRST, so it has to work uniformly for every x.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Just push the negation inward, flipping each quantifier as it passes. ¬∀x ∃y P becomes ∃x ∀y ¬P. The mechanical rule is reliable — you do not need to think about meaning while doing it.

sections.heading: From Single to Nested
sections.explanation:
A nested quantifier is a quantifier in the scope of another quantifier. The expression

  ∀x ∃y P(x, y)

is parsed left to right: first the outer ∀x binds x; then the inner ∃y binds y; finally P(x, y) is evaluated. We can even view nested quantifiers as nested propositional functions: ∀x Q(x), where Q(x) is itself ∃y P(x, y).
examples: ∀x ∀y P(x, y) — 'for every pair (x, y), P holds'.
∀x ∃y P(x, y) — 'for every x, some y makes P(x, y) true; the y can depend on x'.
∃x ∀y P(x, y) — 'there is one x that makes P(x, y) true for ALL y'.
∃x ∃y P(x, y) — 'some pair (x, y) makes P true'.
common_mistakes: Reading nested quantifiers right-to-left. Quantifiers bind in the order they appear; left to right.
Confusing the bound variables with each other. Each variable belongs to its own quantifier.

visual_idea.description: A 2-D grid. The x-axis is the outer variable; the y-axis is the inner variable. Each cell (i, j) is coloured green if P(i, j) holds. Four buttons (∀∀, ∀∃, ∃∀, ∃∃) show which cells the corresponding quantifier inspects.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Toggle a single cell; the four verdict lights at the side update live, dramatizing how a single change affects each pattern differently.

sections.heading: Reading Nested Quantifiers as Loops
sections.explanation:
Nested quantifiers are easy to evaluate if you imagine them as nested loops:

  ∀x ∀y P(x, y)  — like 'for x in U: for y in U: assert P(x, y)'.
  ∀x ∃y P(x, y)  — like 'for x in U: confirm some y in U makes P(x, y)'.
  ∃x ∀y P(x, y)  — like 'find one x in U such that for every y, P(x, y)'.
  ∃x ∃y P(x, y)  — like 'find any pair (x, y) with P(x, y)'.

On a finite domain you can mechanically check each pattern. On an infinite domain you cannot enumerate, but the loop intuition still tells you what the statement claims.
examples: ∀x ∀y (x + y = y + x) over ℝ: every (x, y) commutes — TRUE.
∀x ∃y (x + y = 0) over ℝ: every x has an inverse y = −x — TRUE.
∃y ∀x (x + y = 0) over ℝ: a single y zeros every x — FALSE (no such y).
∃x ∃y (xy = 1) over ℝ: some pair multiplies to 1 — TRUE (x = y = 1).
common_mistakes: Stopping the outer loop too early. ∀ requires verification on every outer value.
Picking a y inside ∃y ∀x that depends on x. In ∃y ∀x, y must be chosen BEFORE x and stay fixed.

visual_idea.description: Two nested loops drawn as concentric rectangles. The outer rectangle is the outer quantifier; the inner one is the inner quantifier. Arrows show the flow of evaluation, and the type of arrow (solid vs dashed) distinguishes ∀ from ∃.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Step the loop one iteration at a time and show which values have been tested or witnessed so far.

sections.heading: The Quantifier Order Trap
sections.explanation:
Same-type quantifiers commute freely. Different-type quantifiers in general do NOT.

  ∀x ∀y P(x, y) ≡ ∀y ∀x P(x, y).
  ∃x ∃y P(x, y) ≡ ∃y ∃x P(x, y).
  ∃y ∀x P(x, y)  ⇒  ∀x ∃y P(x, y)   (one direction only).
  ∀x ∃y P(x, y)  ⇏  ∃y ∀x P(x, y).

The asymmetry is the whole point. ∃y ∀x is STRICTLY STRONGER than ∀x ∃y because the y must work uniformly for every x, not depend on x. This distinction is the difference between continuity and uniform continuity in calculus, and between local and global witnesses everywhere in mathematics.
examples: ∀x ∃y (y > x) over ℤ: TRUE — y = x + 1 always works.
∃y ∀x (y > x) over ℤ: FALSE — no integer is greater than every integer.
∀x ∃y (xy = x) over ℝ: TRUE — for every x, take y = 1.
∃y ∀x (xy = x) over ℝ: TRUE — y = 1 works for every x; the same y.
common_mistakes: Assuming ∀x ∃y and ∃y ∀x are interchangeable. They are NOT in general; the second implies the first, not the reverse.
Writing ∀x ∃y but treating y as fixed independently of x in a proof. y was chosen for THAT x.

visual_idea.description: A 'two-level table': for each outer value of x in ∀x ∃y, a separate inner column shows the witness y chosen for that x — sometimes a different y per row. For ∃y ∀x, all rows share the SAME witness y, highlighted with a single column on the right.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: A toggle marked 'allow y to depend on x' visualizes the added freedom of ∀x ∃y over ∃y ∀x.

sections.heading: Translating Mathematical Statements
sections.explanation:
A typical recipe for translating a mathematical English sentence:

  1. Make implicit quantifiers explicit. 'The sum of two positive integers is positive' really means 'For all positive integers x, y, x + y is positive'.
  2. Choose variable names and a domain.
  3. Use the standard patterns from Lesson 2: 'all A are B' uses → inside ∀; 'some A is B' uses ∧ inside ∃.
  4. Combine with logical connectives. Multiple quantifiers stack from outside-in.

Look out especially for sentences that hide multiple quantifiers behind words like 'always', 'never', and 'for any'.
examples: 'The sum of two positive integers is positive' → ∀x ∀y ((x > 0 ∧ y > 0) → x + y > 0). Domain ℤ.
'There is a woman who has taken a flight on every airline in the world' → ∃w ∀a ∃f (P(w, f) ∧ Q(f, a)) where P is 'has taken' and Q is 'is on airline'.
'Brothers are siblings' → ∀x ∀y (B(x, y) → S(x, y)).
'Everyone loves himself' → ∀x L(x, x).
common_mistakes: Forgetting an implicit ∀. 'Squares of integers are non-negative' means 'For every integer n, n² ≥ 0'.
Using too few variables. Three different objects need three different variable names.

visual_idea.description: A two-column reference: left lists English math sentence patterns ('for any', 'there exists', 'always', 'never', 'sum of any two', 'for some y depending on x'); right lists the corresponding nested-quantifier templates.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click any pattern to see two example translations: a trivial one for warm-up and a course-level one.

sections.heading: Negating Nested Quantifiers
sections.explanation:
To negate a nested-quantifier expression, walk the negation INWARD, flipping each quantifier as you pass it, until ¬ touches the predicate.

  ¬∀x ∃y P(x, y)  ≡  ∃x ¬∃y P(x, y)  ≡  ∃x ∀y ¬P(x, y)
  ¬∃x ∀y P(x, y)  ≡  ∀x ¬∀y P(x, y)  ≡  ∀x ∃y ¬P(x, y)

This procedure is mechanical. You do not need to think about the meaning of the statement until the rewrite is complete; only then translate back into English to check your understanding.
examples: Original: ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0 ∀x (|x − a| < δ → |f(x) − L| < ε)  (limit definition).
Negation: ∃ε > 0 ∀δ > 0 ∃x (|x − a| < δ ∧ |f(x) − L| ≥ ε).
Original: ∃w ∀a ∃f (P(w, f) ∧ Q(f, a))  ('a woman has taken a flight on every airline').
Negation: ∀w ∃a ∀f (¬P(w, f) ∨ ¬Q(f, a))  ('every woman has some airline such that no flight she took is on it').
common_mistakes: Forgetting to negate the inner predicate. The final step always negates whatever was inside the innermost quantifier.
Stopping after one flip. Every quantifier in the chain must flip when ¬ moves past it.

visual_idea.description: A vertical rewrite chain: at the top is the original nested expression. Each downward step shows ¬ moving past one quantifier, with the rule label 'De Morgan for ∀' or 'De Morgan for ∃' on the right.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: The user clicks 'next step' to advance the negation by one quantifier, animating the flip.

worked_examples.problem: Domain = real numbers. Determine the truth value of (a) ∀x ∀y (x + y = y + x), (b) ∀x ∃y (x + y = 0), (c) ∃y ∀x (x + y = 0).
step_by_step_solution: (a) Addition of reals is commutative. Every (x, y) satisfies x + y = y + x. ∀∀ holds.
(b) For each x, take y = −x; then x + y = 0. So every x has a witness y, and ∀∃ holds.
(c) We need ONE y that zeros every x. For y = 0, x + 0 = x, not 0 in general. For any other y, just pick x ≠ −y. No uniform witness exists. ∃∀ fails.
worked_examples.why_it_works: (b) and (c) differ exactly in whether y is allowed to depend on x. With ∀x ∃y, y can be a function of x; with ∃y ∀x, y must be a constant good for every x.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Mistakenly answering (c) TRUE because (b) is true. ∃∀ is strictly stronger than ∀∃ — true for one is not true for the other.

worked_examples.problem: Translate: 'Every student in your school has taken a course in chemistry.' Use S(x) = 'x is a student in your school', C(x, y) = 'x has taken course y', U(y) = 'y is a course in chemistry'. Domain = all people and all courses.
step_by_step_solution: Identify the implicit quantifiers. 'Every student' ⇒ ∀x with filter S(x). 'Has taken a chemistry course' ⇒ ∃y with filter U(y).
Combine: ∀x (S(x) → ∃y (U(y) ∧ C(x, y))).
Confirm: for each student x, there exists a chemistry course y that x took.
worked_examples.why_it_works: The outer ∀ ranges over all people; S(x) filters to students. The inner ∃ ranges over courses; U(y) filters to chemistry courses; C(x, y) is the relation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Putting the existential outside the universal: ∃y (U(y) ∧ ∀x (S(x) → C(x, y))) wrongly says there is ONE chemistry course that every student took.

worked_examples.problem: Negate ∀x ∃y (P(x, y) → Q(x, y)) so that ¬ touches only predicates.
step_by_step_solution: Push ¬ past the outer ∀: ∃x ¬∃y (P(x, y) → Q(x, y)).
Push ¬ past the inner ∃: ∃x ∀y ¬(P(x, y) → Q(x, y)).
Use ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q: ∃x ∀y (P(x, y) ∧ ¬Q(x, y)).
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each quantifier flips when ¬ passes it, and the inner implication is rewritten as a conjunction with negated consequent.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing ∃x ∀y (P(x, y) → ¬Q(x, y)). The negation of an implication is NOT another implication — it is a conjunction.

quick_checks.question: Over the integers, which is TRUE?
quick_checks.explanation: For every integer x, take y = x + 1. The other options fail: no single y is greater than every x; no x is less than every y.

quick_checks.question: Negate ∃x ∀y P(x, y) so that ¬ touches only the predicate:
quick_checks.explanation: Flip ∃ to ∀ and ∀ to ∃, then negate the predicate.

quick_checks.question: ∀x ∃y P(x, y) implies ∃y ∀x P(x, y).
quick_checks.explanation: The reverse direction holds, but not this one. A per-x witness need not be uniform across x.

key_takeaways: Same-type quantifiers commute freely; mixed-type quantifiers (∀∃ vs ∃∀) generally do not.
∃y ∀x P(x, y) ⇒ ∀x ∃y P(x, y), but the reverse fails.
In ∀x ∃y, the y can depend on x; in ∃y ∀x, the y must be a single witness for every x.
Push ¬ inward step by step, flipping each quantifier; the final result has ¬ touching only atomic predicates.
Implicit quantifiers in math English ('always', 'for any', 'sum of any two') must be made explicit before translating.
summary.next: You are now ready for the Module 2 exercises page, where you will practice translating, evaluating, and negating quantified statements with multiple-choice, true/false, short-answer, step-by-step, and randomized drills.

exercises.title: Module 2 Exercises — Predicate Logic
exercises.description: Practice problems covering Module 2: predicates, quantifiers, translation between English and predicate logic, De Morgan's laws for quantifiers, and nested-quantifier evaluation and negation. Includes MCQ, true/false, short answer, step-by-step questions, exam-style problems, and randomized templates for unlimited practice.

questions.question: P(x) is 'x > 5'. Which is a proposition?
questions.explanation: Plugging a specific value into the predicate gives a proposition: '7 > 5' is true.

questions.question: Domain = ℤ. Which is TRUE?
questions.explanation: 0 is the additive identity. The first fails for n = 0; the second has no witness; the last requires a single n that zeros every m.

questions.question: 'All birds fly' translates to:
questions.explanation: 'All A are B' uses implication inside ∀.

questions.question: 'Some integer is even' translates to:
questions.explanation: On the integer domain we just say 'there exists n with E(n)'.

questions.question: Negate ∀x P(x):
questions.explanation: De Morgan for quantifiers: flip ∀ to ∃ and negate the predicate.

questions.question: Domain = ℝ. ∀x ∃y (x + y = 0) is:
questions.explanation: Every real has an additive inverse.

questions.question: Domain = ℝ. ∃y ∀x (x + y = 0) is:
choices: False — no single y zeros every x
questions.answer: False — no single y zeros every x
questions.explanation: ∃∀ is strictly stronger than ∀∃; here it fails because no real is the inverse of every real.

questions.question: What is the negation of 'No student is late'?
A predicate P(x) by itself is a proposition.
questions.explanation: It becomes a proposition only when x is replaced by a value or bound by a quantifier.

questions.question: On the empty domain, ∀x P(x) is true.
questions.explanation: Vacuously true: there is no element that fails the predicate.

questions.question: ∀x ∀y P(x, y) is logically equivalent to ∀y ∀x P(x, y).
questions.explanation: Same-type quantifiers commute.

questions.question: ∀x ∃y P(x, y) is logically equivalent to ∃y ∀x P(x, y).
questions.explanation: Different-type quantifiers in general do not commute. ∃∀ is strictly stronger.

questions.question: ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x).
questions.explanation: De Morgan for quantifiers.

questions.question: 'Every student passed' is correctly translated as ∀x (S(x) ∧ P(x)).
questions.explanation: Using ∧ would force every domain element to be a student. The correct form is ∀x (S(x) → P(x)).

questions.question: ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q.
questions.explanation: Standard equivalence; vital when negating ∀ A → B forms.

questions.question: What is a 'domain of discourse' and why must it be specified?
questions.answer: The domain of discourse is the set of all objects the quantified variables can take values from. The truth value of a quantified statement depends critically on the domain — the same predicate may be true on one domain and false on another — so the domain must always be stated.
questions.explanation: Predicates have no fixed meaning outside a stated domain.

questions.question: Translate 'There is a student in this class who has visited Mexico'. Use C(x) = 'x is in this class', S(x) = 'x is a student', M(x) = 'x has visited Mexico'.
questions.answer: Domain restricted to students in this class: ∃x M(x). Unrestricted domain: ∃x (S(x) ∧ C(x) ∧ M(x)).
questions.explanation: Existential with conjunctive filter.

questions.question: Express the negation of 'Every Swedish movie is serious' so that ¬ touches only predicates.
questions.answer: Original: ∀x (S(x) → R(x)). Negation: ∃x (S(x) ∧ ¬R(x)) — 'some Swedish movie is not serious'.
questions.explanation: Flip ∀ to ∃, then ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q.

questions.question: Why does ∃y ∀x P(x, y) imply ∀x ∃y P(x, y), but not the other way around?
questions.answer: If a single y witnesses P for every x, then for each x we can use that same y. This gives ∀x ∃y. The converse fails because ∀x ∃y allows the witness y to change with x — there might be no single y that works for all of them simultaneously.
questions.explanation: Uniform-witness ⇒ per-x witness, but per-x witness need not be uniform.

questions.question: Make the implicit quantifiers explicit and translate: 'The product of two negative numbers is positive.'
questions.explanation: 'The product of two' hides ∀x ∀y; 'is positive' is the conclusion of an implication filtered by the sign hypothesis.

questions.question: Express 'No driver disobeys the speed limit' using D(x) and O(x), then negate the result so ¬ touches only predicates.
questions.answer:
Step 1. 'No A is B': ¬∃x (D(x) ∧ ¬O(x)) ≡ ∀x (D(x) → O(x)).
Step 2. Negate: ¬∀x (D(x) → O(x)).
Step 3. Push past ∀: ∃x ¬(D(x) → O(x)).
Step 4. Use ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q: ∃x (D(x) ∧ ¬O(x)).
Final: 'Some driver disobeys the speed limit'.
questions.explanation: Two-step rewrite: translate, then negate using De Morgan plus the implication-as-conjunction trick.

questions.question: On a finite domain U = {1, 2, 3} with P(x, y) true exactly for (1, 3), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3), determine the truth value of (a) ∀y ∃x (x ≠ y ∧ P(x, y)), (b) ∀x ∃y (x ≠ y ∧ ¬P(x, y)).
questions.answer:
(a) For y = 1: x ∈ {2, 3} both work since (2,1) and (3,1) are true. For y = 2: (3, 2) is true. For y = 3: (1, 3) is true. ∀y holds. TRUE.
(b) For x = 1: need y ≠ 1 with ¬P(1, y). P(1, 2) is false (not in list) and 2 ≠ 1. ✓. For x = 2: need y ≠ 2 with ¬P(2, y). y = 3: (2, 3) is not in list, ¬P(2, 3) holds. ✓. For x = 3: need y ≠ 3 with ¬P(3, y). y = 1: P(3, 1) is in list, fails. y = 2: P(3, 2) is in list, fails. No witness. ✗. FALSE.
questions.explanation: Mechanical evaluation on a finite domain confirms why ∀∃ requires a witness for every outer value.

questions.question: Translate 'Every student in your class has visited at least one country in Europe' using S(x), C(y), V(x, y). Domain = all people and all countries.
questions.explanation: Outer ∀ over students (with filter), inner ∃ over countries (with filter), joined by the visit relation.

questions.question: Negate ∀x ∃y ∀z P(x, y, z) so that ¬ touches only the predicate.
questions.answer:
¬∀x ∃y ∀z P(x, y, z)
≡ ∃x ¬∃y ∀z P(x, y, z)
≡ ∃x ∀y ¬∀z P(x, y, z)
≡ ∃x ∀y ∃z ¬P(x, y, z).
questions.explanation: Each pass of the negation flips one quantifier; three passes for three quantifiers.

questions.question: Let S(x) = 'x is a student', F(x) = 'x is a faculty member', A(x, y) = 'x has asked y a question'. Domain = all people. Translate: 'Some student has not asked any faculty member a question.'
questions.explanation: Outer ∃ over students; inner ∀ over faculty with negated relation.

questions.question: Determine the truth value of each over the integers: (a) ∀n ∃m (n² < m). (b) ∃n ∀m (n < m²). (c) ∀n ∃m (n + m = 0). (d) ∃n ∀m (nm = m).
questions.answer:
(a) TRUE — given n, take m = n² + 1.
(b) TRUE — n = 0 satisfies 0 < m² for every m ≠ 0; for m = 0 the predicate becomes 0 < 0 which is false. Re-examining: with m allowed to be 0, n = 0 fails. Try n = -1: -1 < m² holds for every m (m² ≥ 0 > -1). TRUE.
(c) TRUE — for each n, take m = -n.
(d) TRUE — n = 1 gives 1 · m = m for every m.
questions.explanation: Each statement requires a witness or universal verification; counterexamples or witnesses settle the result.

questions.question: Express the negation of 'For every positive integer n, there is a prime greater than n' so that ¬ touches only predicates.
questions.answer:
Original: ∀n (n > 0 → ∃p (Prime(p) ∧ p > n)).
Negation: ∃n (n > 0 ∧ ∀p (¬Prime(p) ∨ p ≤ n)) ≡ ∃n (n > 0 ∧ ∀p (Prime(p) → p ≤ n)) — 'there is a positive integer n such that every prime is at most n'.
questions.explanation: After flipping ∀ to ∃ and ∃ to ∀, ¬(Prime ∧ p > n) becomes ¬Prime ∨ p ≤ n, equivalently Prime → p ≤ n.

questions.question: Find the truth value of ∀x ∃y (xy = 1) over (a) the real numbers, (b) the positive real numbers, (c) the integers.
questions.answer:
(a) FALSE — x = 0 has no inverse.
(b) TRUE — for every positive real x, take y = 1/x.
(c) FALSE — only x = ±1 have integer inverses; e.g., x = 2 has no integer y with 2y = 1.
questions.explanation: The same formula has different truth values on different domains.

questions.question: Use quantifiers to express: 'There is a course that every student in your school has taken.' Use S(x) for 'x is a student in your school', C(y) for 'y is a course', T(x, y) for 'x has taken y'. Domain = all people and all courses.
questions.explanation: ∃ outside, ∀ inside, because we want one specific course taken by every student.

questions.template: Domain = {DOMAIN}. Determine the truth value of {EXPR}.
questions.instructions: Pick one DOMAIN and one EXPR; evaluate by giving a witness or counterexample. Cycle through random pairs to drill the most common nested-quantifier patterns.
questions.example_realization: Realization: DOMAIN = ℤ, EXPR = '∀x ∃y (xy = 1)'. Answer: FALSE (x = 2 has no integer inverse).
questions.explanation: Repeated random drill builds intuition for how the same expression behaves on different domains.

questions.template: Translate the English sentence into predicate logic: '{SENTENCE}'. Use predicates {PREDS}, domain = {DOMAIN}.

SENTENCE: Every prime greater than 2 is odd.
Some integer is both prime and even.

questions.instructions: Apply 'all A are B' → ∀x (A(x) → B(x)) and 'some A is B' → ∃x (A(x) ∧ B(x)). 'No A is B' is the negation of an existential.
questions.example_realization: Realization: SENTENCE = 'No bird is mute.' Translation: ∀x (B(x) → ¬M(x)).
questions.explanation: Random drill on the standard translation patterns prevents the most common conjunction-vs-implication mistake.

questions.template: Negate {EXPR} so that ¬ touches only predicates.
questions.instructions: Flip every quantifier in turn and negate the innermost predicate. Use ¬(P → Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q and De Morgan for ∧/∨ as needed.
questions.explanation: Drilling negation step-by-step locks in the mechanical procedure.

questions.template: On a finite domain U = {DOMAIN_SET}, evaluate {EXPR} where P(x, y) is true exactly for the listed pairs: {PAIRS}.
questions.instructions: Iterate over the domain mechanically: for ∀ check every outer value; for ∃ search for any witness.
questions.example_realization: Realization: domain {1,2,3}, EXPR = '∀x ∃y P(x, y)', pairs (1,1),(2,2),(3,3). Each x has the witness y = x. TRUE.
questions.explanation: Direct enumeration on small finite domains makes the loop intuition concrete.
